parameters.quote: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, smoke, fire, or thermal runaway to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, including incidents with no injury or property damage. The manufacturer must notify affected customers within 72 hours when the incident presents a credible safety risk to their unit or requires customer action; urgent hazards require immediate notice.

S1_incident_reporting.rule_summary: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, smoke, fire, or thermal runaway to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, including incidents with no injury or property damage. The manufacturer must notify affected customers within 72 hours when the incident presents a credible safety risk to their unit or requires customer action; urgent hazards require immediate notice.
S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, smoke, fire, or thermal runaway to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, including incidents with no injury or property damage. A follow-up report with investigation findings and any corrective action is due within 30 days. The manufacturer must notify affected customers within 72 hours when the incident presents a credible safety risk to their unit or requires customer action; urgent hazards require immediate notice. Reports must identify the model and known circumstances, while protecting personal information.

S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: Manufacturers must provide full per-model results to regulators and to customers who buy that model, including the test method, sample size, failure rate, and relevant limitations. No fixed failure-rate threshold alone automatically prohibits a model from being newly placed on the market.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55°C using a regulator-recognized protocol, with results calculated from a statistically representative sample and retained for audit. Manufacturers must provide full per-model results to regulators and to customers who buy that model, including the test method, sample size, failure rate, and relevant limitations. Regulators may require corrective action, restrictions, or retesting based on test results and relevant incident evidence. No fixed failure-rate threshold alone automatically prohibits a model from being newly placed on the market.

S3_remote_shutoff.rule_summary: All new home battery units placed on the market must support remote emergency shut-off within 24 months after adoption, with a secure mechanism accessible to authorized emergency responders and the customer. S3_remote_shutoff.final_rule_text: All new home battery units placed on the market must support remote emergency shut-off within 24 months after adoption, with a secure mechanism accessible to authorized emergency responders and the customer. Manufacturers must provide an upgrade plan for installed units and enable shut-off for units technically capable of receiving it within 6 years after adoption. Any limitations and safe-use instructions must be disclosed to customers.

S4_fire_suppression.final_rule_text: Built-in fire suppression is required on all new home battery units placed on the market beginning 36 months after adoption. The requirement applies to each model and must be verified through testing demonstrating that the suppression system operates as intended. Manufacturers must disclose the presence and relevant limitations of the system to customers.

parameters.quote: When a model's verified thermal-incident rate exceeds 8 incidents per 100,000 installed units in any rolling 12-month period, the manufacturer must promptly notify the regulator and affected customers. The threshold triggers regulator investigation and a corrective-action determination; a mandatory recall with an effective remedy is required when that determination establishes a material safety risk requiring recall.

S5_customer_disclosure.rule_summary: When a model's verified thermal-incident rate exceeds 8 incidents per 100,000 installed units in any rolling 12-month period, the manufacturer must promptly notify the regulator and affected customers. The threshold triggers regulator investigation and a corrective-action determination; a mandatory recall with an effective remedy is required when that determination establishes a material safety risk requiring recall.
S5_customer_disclosure.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must provide customers with model-specific safety notices, including known hazards, required safe-use measures, and any corrective actions, and promptly update notices when material safety information changes. When a model’s verified thermal-incident rate exceeds 8 incidents per 100,000 installed units in any rolling 12-month period, the manufacturer must promptly notify the regulator and affected customers. Rates must use documented incident counts and installed-unit denominators; regulators may audit the data and require correction of undercounts. The threshold triggers regulator investigation and a corrective-action determination; a mandatory recall with an effective remedy is required when that determination establishes a material safety risk requiring recall. Regulators may impose additional restrictions where warranted; a recall does not by itself constitute a permanent market ban.

judge_section_notes: The final S2 drops any numeric failure-rate cap and sales stop, which is the largest gain for Northwind's Hearth 10 (6.2%), while per-model results still go to customers and regulators, not the public. S5 sets an 8/100k investigation trigger but makes recall conditional on a regulator determination with no automatic recall, which weakens the rule for Halcyon's Ember 8 (9.9).
